title: George Frazier's 1941 Down Beat review of the band at Nick's
summary: Johnston reads Frazier's praise of McPartland's band at Nick's.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Critics, polls and the jazz press

blocks.x: Well I think it's important, it's important to have the record include the fact that you have been written about in just about every important magazine or paper that has anything to say about jazz.
Those jazz history books are very good, but the Down Beat I see you have there, the
Down Beat has been carrying on about jazz for years you know. And I've been written up in there quite a bit I know.
Well this one goes back thirty years really. Because this is June 15th 1941.
Just before I went in the Army. Jack Teagarden, and then I went in the Army.

And I would like to read a little bit of this because sometimes when, when people just listen to us be excited about people we're interviewing, they think that we haven't given them a balanced account. And I don't think that's so with this particular interview. But I like this because although he is very, I like it because he is very honest and even though he has to say something that's not, ...

..... then he comes up and could not praise you any more than he does. And this is George Frazier and he says, 'the band that Jimmy McPartland had at Nicks was a quite magnificent little band indeed. And the news that it is there no longer can hardly be called glad tidings. Now I think that is a splendid beginning. (LAUGHTER).' It wasn't a flawless band and it's shortcomings were nothing if not palpable. But it's conception was absolutely perfect.

And in it's high, sensitive moments, it produced lovely unforgettable jazz." Jimmy this is really sincere and high praise. "For my money, it was a more thrilling affair than Red Allen's at Cafe Society and I say that in full realisation that Red's is one of the very best small bands ever.
"McPartland's was a rough band and at times an unforgivably sloppy one, but at its best on a good night when the guys were feeling right, it was practically unbeatable." (LAUGHTER).
I think that goes the same for any band really. And I'm glad that he wrote that because you don't always play well. You can't always play well. I assure you of that.

"And Jimmy of course, was a treat to hear with that big masculine tone that crispness and that lovely singing style. And he had a freshness and an enthusiasm that a man has only when he's very, very new to 7th Avenue and 10th and believes that God's in his heaven and Nick is one of the sweetest guys in the trade and a really lovely character." (LAUGHTER).
I don't know about Frdzier, everything is lovely for him isn't it? (LAUGHTER).
Yes, he uses it many, many times. No, but I just think that that's a marvellous thing for people to know later on.

Well he understands there because a musician, everytime you get up on that bandstand or you're going to play a concert or whatever you're, it doesn't make any difference what you're playing for, you know you're going to try the best, your best if you're a dedicated musician. You can't let down. Your art is your musical integrity is the tops or else you're not a musician. Or an artist or whatever you want to call them.

So you do try your best at all times, but it just does not come out that way all the time, I'll assure you. You'd have high hopes, and you do reach your highs and you do reach your lows. You just can't play well all the time. I can't, I don't think anyone can really.

I'm very glad for more reasons than one, that we have put several of your recordings on tape here. But this next sentence makes me especially glad. He says, 'the tragedy is no one bothered to record McPartland during those weeks when the whole band seemed revitalised by his presence and sounded better than it has in ages and ages.'
